title: A woman clothed with the sun (Apocalypse 12)
hookLine: the moon under her feet and twelve stars; read on the Assumption as Mary and the Church

lines: THE ARK, LOST WITH THE TEMPLE.
cards: Nearly six hundred years before Christ, Babylon's army burned the temple in Jerusalem.
After that, the ark of the covenant, the gold-covered chest that held the tablets of the law, is never seen again in the Bible's history.
One old story, in Second Maccabees, says the prophet Jeremiah hid it in a cave on a mountain until God gathers his people again.
Then, at the very end of Apocalypse eleven, John sees God's temple in heaven open, and there it is: the ark. The very next thing he sees isn't a chest at all. It's a woman.

teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "A woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars." She's about to give birth, crying out in pain.

teach.h: A WOMAN, A CHILD, A DRAGON.
teach.b: Then a second sign: a great red dragon, with seven heads and ten horns, waiting to devour the child as soon as it's born. The child, a son who will rule all the nations, is born and caught up to God and to his throne.
The woman flees into the wilderness, to a place God has prepared for her. Then war breaks out in heaven, Michael and his angels against the dragon, and the dragon is thrown down.
The text names him: that old serpent, the devil.
That reaches back to Genesis, where God tells the serpent there will be enmity between him and the woman, between his seed and hers. Who is the woman? Catholic tradition doesn't pick just one answer.
She is Mary, who bore the child who rules the nations; the Church reads this passage on the feast of the Assumption, in August.
She is also the Church, the people of God, who bring Christ into the world in pain and are kept safe in the wilderness. Many readers also see Israel in her twelve stars, the twelve tribes.
The symbols carry more than one meaning at once.

teach.h: A WOMAN CLOTHED WITH THE SUN.
teach.b: And remember how the scene began: with the ark of the covenant. Catholic tradition has long called Mary the ark of the new covenant, the one who carried God within her.

how: Catholics hear Apocalypse 12 on the Solemnity of the Assumption, August 15, and Marian art, especially images of the Immaculate Conception, often shows Mary with the sun, the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars.

o: the angel who tells Mary she will bear a son
the prophet who hid the ark in a mountain cave
the archangel who fights the dragon and throws it down

games.q: the woman and the dragon — tap the pairs.

s: the ark of the covenant appears just before the woman
Apocalypse 11:19: God's temple in heaven opens and the ark is seen; then the woman.
Catholic tradition says the woman can only be Mary
it reads her as Mary and as the Church, and many readers also see Israel.
the dragon is named as that old serpent, linking back to Genesis
the enmity between the serpent and the woman in Genesis 3.

games.q: someone asks you who the woman clothed with the sun really is. in Catholic tradition, what's the answer?
o: Mary and the Church, with Israel in view too: more than one at once.
games.why: the Church reads Apocalypse 12 on the Assumption, about Mary, and also hears in it the Church bringing Christ into the world; the twelve stars recall Israel's tribes.

practice: If the moon is up, go to a window; if not, picture it on a clear night.

Imagine it under someone's feet, the sun around her, twelve stars over her head, the whole sky as clothing, then remember she was also a mother in pain, with a dragon in front of her, and she was kept safe.
If you pray, you can ask Mary to pray for you; if not, just stay with the sky.

wordCard.voice: Michael, the archangel. Apocalypse twelve: he and his angels throw the ancient dragon, that old serpent, out of heaven. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a woman clothed with the sun (Apocalypse 12:1).

carryVoice: Your line: clothed with the sun. One sign, more than one meaning. Day six hundred twenty-seven, done.
